paragraphs: The paper examines how the examples people encounter during testing can change their category judgments. Its central finding is that identical training need not produce identical answers afterward. Depending on the other test objects presented, people can be led to classify a particular object in opposite ways, even though they receive no feedback identifying correct labels.

The authors call this the Test-Item Effect and identify two ways to induce it: changing the order of test examples or changing their distribution. This makes the testing environment part of the explanation of behavior. A response reflects both earlier labeled training and the unlabeled examples encountered while making subsequent judgments.

To model this effect, the paper treats categorization as online semi-supervised learning: learning continues as unlabeled test items arrive. It extends three established models of human category learning to account for that process. The contribution connects an observed dependence on test context with a learning framework that can represent changes occurring without corrective feedback.
icml-2010-cognitive-models-of-test-item-.tldr: Unlabeled test examples can change human category judgments, and extensions of three cognitive models explain this as ongoing semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces conditional topic random fields to combine two capabilities in topic modeling: using rich information about words and documents, and representing dependence between neighboring words’ topic assignments. The motivation is that the generative topic models discussed in the abstract do not handle both capabilities together, restricting the information their topic assignments can reflect.

The model accepts arbitrary nonlocal features, so its inputs need not concern only an individual word in isolation. It also incorporates a Markov dependency between adjacent topic assignments. For computation, the authors develop a variational inference algorithm whose cost scales linearly with the number of topics, together with a maximum likelihood procedure for learning parameters.

For supervised applications, the paper additionally proposes max-margin training, described as potentially more discriminative. Experiments use real review-rating data and show advantages over generative competitors, as well as advantages of max-margin training over maximum likelihood. These findings support combining richer contextual features, local topic dependencies, and a supervised training objective in the evaluated setting.
icml-2010-conditional-topic-random-field.tldr: Conditional topic random fields combine rich contextual features with neighboring topic dependencies and show benefits on review-rating data.

paragraphs: Maximum entropy provides a framework for constructing statistical models, but applying it to interactions requires accounting for when information becomes available. In a sequential setting, information may be revealed gradually and influence later decisions. Feedback adds another connection between what happens now and what can be observed or chosen afterward.

The paper introduces maximum causal entropy to represent these information relationships. Its foundation is causally conditioned probabilities, which account for the availability and influence of sequentially revealed side information. The key modeling concern is therefore the timing of information: a description of sequential behavior must reflect what was available at the relevant point in the interaction.

Using this principle, the authors derive models for sequential data involving revealed information, interaction, and feedback. They demonstrate its applicability to statistical formulations of inverse optimal control and decision prediction. The contribution supplies a framework for these tasks that explicitly incorporates information flow, extending the reach of entropy-based modeling to the interactive settings considered.
icml-2010-modeling-interaction-via-the-p.tldr: Maximum causal entropy extends entropy-based modeling to sequential interactions by accounting for when information becomes available.

paragraphs: The paper studies how knowledge learned from substantial source-domain training data can help a supervised learner operating online in a target domain. The target learner receives data over time, and the proposed Online Transfer Learning framework aims to use previously learned knowledge to improve that continuing learning process.

A central challenge is that the source and target need not share class distributions or the same data-generating distribution. They may also describe examples through different features. The authors address both homogeneous transfer, involving compatible feature representations, and heterogeneous transfer, where the representations differ. This distinction makes feature mismatch an explicit part of the transfer problem.

The paper proposes algorithms for these two settings and establishes mistake bounds, providing theoretical statements about their prediction errors during online learning. It also evaluates the techniques on several challenging transfer tasks and reports encouraging results. Together, the analysis and experiments support the usefulness of transferring prior knowledge in the studied settings despite differences between source and target data.
icml-2010-otl-a-framework-of-online-tran.tldr: Online Transfer Learning uses source-domain knowledge to support online target learning even when distributions or feature representations differ.

paragraphs: The paper addresses Bayesian inference for models whose likelihood functions cannot be evaluated tractably. Such models occur in the natural and social sciences. Approximate Bayesian Computation makes inference possible in this setting, but the abstract describes existing approaches as computationally demanding and difficult to configure, especially when prior information is limited.

Two practical obstacles motivate the work: selecting suitable summary statistics and tuning the inference algorithm. The authors adapt Expectation Propagation, an approximate inference technique, to the likelihood-free setting. The resulting ABC-EP algorithm does not require summary statistics, removing the need to choose those summaries as part of preparing the inference procedure.

The abstract reports that the algorithm is an order of magnitude faster than existing techniques and remains usable with vague prior information. These claims address both computational cost and practical setup. The contribution is an approximate Bayesian method that broadens the available tools for otherwise intractable models while directly tackling several usability problems identified for likelihood-free inference.
icml-2011-abc-ep-expectation-propagation.tldr: ABC-EP adapts Expectation Propagation to likelihood-free inference, avoiding summary statistics and reporting an order-of-magnitude speed improvement.

paragraphs: Nonlinear support vector machines can become costly to use for prediction because their computation grows linearly with the number of support vectors. The paper targets this prediction bottleneck with AdaptSVM, an algorithm that approximates kernel computations while retaining a mechanism for returning to the original calculation when needed.

AdaptSVM selectively reduces the support vectors involved in kernel computation and adds a correction term that is inexpensive to compute online. It also uses an estimated variance and a maximum error tolerance to decide when to fall back to the original kernel computation. This makes the amount of approximation responsive to its estimated reliability.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and a performance guarantee, then evaluate the method on multiple large-scale datasets. They report prediction speedups reaching 10,000 times with an accuracy loss below 0.5, without specifying the accuracy unit in the abstract. This is a reported maximum speedup, not a uniform improvement across every prediction problem; the adaptive fallback is part of the proposed approach.
icml-2011-adaptive-kernel-approximation-.tldr: AdaptSVM accelerates nonlinear SVM prediction through corrected kernel approximations and adaptive fallback based on estimated uncertainty and error tolerance.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations becomes more complicated when the demonstrations express different objectives. This paper considers unlabeled behavior trajectories generated by varying intentions. The learner must discover which trajectories belong together and infer the objectives behind them, without receiving intention labels that would separate the demonstrations in advance.

The authors derive an expectation-maximization approach that groups trajectories while using inverse reinforcement learning to infer an objective for each group. Several inverse reinforcement learning methods can serve within this framework. Once the clusters have been constructed, they are used to identify a trajectory’s intention quickly, connecting objective discovery with subsequent recognition.

The paper also examines a likelihood-based inverse reinforcement learning method that adjusts reward parameters through gradient ascent. It reports success in quickly identifying unknown reward functions. A demonstration in a simple highway car simulator shows the approach acquiring a human driver’s preferences. This supports the proposed combination of clustering and reward inference within the stated apprenticeship-learning example.
icml-2011-apprenticeship-learning-about-.tldr: The paper combines trajectory clustering and inverse reinforcement learning to discover and recognize multiple intentions in unlabeled demonstrations.

paragraphs: Co-training uses two classifiers trained on different views of the same data. Each classifier supplies confident predictions on unlabeled examples to help teach the other. This paper addresses a practical obstacle to that arrangement: many learning problems provide a single feature representation without an explicit division into two useful views.

The authors introduce an algorithm that splits the feature space during learning. The split is chosen specifically to encourage successful co-training, drawing inspiration from an existing theoretical analysis. Constructing the views becomes part of the learning procedure, allowing the two-classifier teaching process to be applied when a suitable multi-view representation is not already supplied.

The method is evaluated in a weakly supervised object-recognition setting on Caltech-256. The abstract reports significant improvements over the cited previous results in almost all training-set size settings. These findings support the effectiveness of the learned feature decomposition for that task and show how co-training can be extended beyond problems with an explicit multi-view input representation.
icml-2011-automatic-feature-decompositio.tldr: The method learns a feature split that enables co-training from a single view and improves weakly supervised object recognition in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: The paper clusters samples using their pairwise similarities. It seeks a factorization of the similarity matrix into a cluster-probability matrix multiplied by its transpose. This represents similarities through probabilistic cluster memberships, making the relationship between the observed similarities and the proposed grouping part of a single matrix decomposition.

The authors introduce a rotation-based algorithm to compute this left-stochastic decomposition. They also establish a theoretical connection with soft kernel k-means clustering. That connection relates the proposed factorization to a clustering formulation with soft assignments, giving a second way to understand what the decomposition represents and how it serves the grouping task.

The theoretical results include error bounds and conditions under which both the factorization and the clustering are unique. Uniqueness is therefore conditional rather than a claim about every similarity matrix. Experiments on simulated and real similarity datasets report reliable, accurate clusterings. The paper combines a concrete computational method with analysis of its relationship to clustering, its ambiguity, and its errors.
icml-2011-clustering-by-left-stochastic-.tldr: Left-stochastic matrix factorization derives probabilistic clusters from pairwise similarities, with conditional uniqueness results, error bounds, and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: Training restricted Boltzmann machines can depend heavily on learning-rate schedules, initial weight scales, and the representation of binary data. The paper highlights a specific inconsistency: flipping some bits and adjusting weights and biases can produce an equivalent model, yet traditional learning rules can behave differently under that change of representation.

The authors derive an enhanced gradient that is invariant to these bit-flipping transformations. This targets a source of training sensitivity tied to equivalent ways of expressing the same model. They also propose automatic learning-rate adjustment by maximizing a local estimate of likelihood, addressing the separate difficulty of choosing suitable update sizes during training.

Experiments show that the proposed changes produce more stable RBM training. The two contributions address distinct aspects of the optimization process: how the update direction responds to representation and how its learning rate is selected. The reported finding supports improved stability, while the abstract’s discussion of plateaus and divergence explains why these changes matter for practical training.
icml-2011-enhanced-gradient-and-adaptive.tldr: A bit-flip-invariant gradient and automatic learning-rate adjustment make restricted Boltzmann machine training more stable in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning functions that transform one string into another. Its representations are a class of inversion transduction grammars implementing context-free transducers. The central contribution is a polynomial algorithm for learning this class, presented as the first such result. The claim concerns a specified learnable class of grammars rather than every possible string transformation.

The learnable transductions strictly include all subsequential transductions. In other words, the class covers that entire existing family and extends beyond it. This inclusion describes the expressive reach of the learning result: its significance rests on both the algorithm’s polynomial computation and the range of string-to-string functions that it can learn.

The algorithms build on a generalization of distributional learning. Their correctness is proved under an identification-in-the-limit model, so the guarantee is tied to that formal account of learning. The paper’s stated contribution is theoretical: it establishes a computational learning method and proves correctness for the designated class within the specified learning model.
icml-2011-inference-of-inversion-transdu.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial learning algorithm for a class of inversion transduction grammars, with correctness under identification in the limit.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a gaze-driven model that tracks objects and recognizes them simultaneously. Its observations resemble retinal images: resolution decreases away from the gaze location. This makes attention relevant to the information available for both tasks, since different gaze choices change which parts of the scene are represented most clearly.

Two interacting pathways divide the work. A ventral pathway models object appearance and classification with deep factored restricted Boltzmann machines. A dorsal pathway models location, orientation, scale, and speed, using particle filtering to estimate uncertainty over these states. An attentional mechanism within the dorsal pathway learns to control gaze with the aim of reducing tracking uncertainty.

The architecture connects recognition, motion-state estimation, and the choice of where to look within one modular approach. The authors describe its components as replaceable, its implementation as straightforward, and its computation as practically efficient. They report that it works well on simple video sequences, which is the stated scope of the practical success described in the abstract.
icml-2011-learning-attentional-policies-.tldr: A modular two-pathway model combines recognition and tracking with learned gaze control that aims to reduce tracking uncertainty.

paragraphs: The paper investigates simpler multiplicative updates for learning linear functions online. Starting from the Exponentiated Gradient algorithm, it replaces exponentiation with quadratic or linear functions. The aim is to simplify the operations used in learning while reducing dependence on the parameter that specifies the total sum of the model’s weights.

Both proposed update families reduce that dependence. The linear multiplicative update goes further by placing no restriction on the sum of the weights. Under a wide range of conditions, it achieves worst-case behavior close to Exponentiated Gradient. This is a qualified theoretical comparison: the closeness is established under the conditions considered in the analysis.

The authors analyze square and absolute losses across regression and classification. They also describe experiments in which their algorithms perform comparably to Exponentiated Gradient and the p-norm algorithm. The contribution shows that simpler update operations can retain competitive behavior in the studied settings, combining theoretical analysis with empirical comparisons across alternative online learning rules.
icml-2011-learning-linear-functions-with.tldr: Quadratic and linear multiplicative updates simplify online linear learning while retaining performance comparable to established methods in the studied settings.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to choose training losses for scoring functions used in label ranking. A scoring function produces an ordering, but the loss optimized during training must connect appropriately to the metric used to judge that ordering. The authors extend the notion of order-preserving losses from multiclass classification to ranking.

They show that these losses yield consistent formulations for a family of ranking metrics. A loss can be tailored to a particular metric through weights that depend on both the metric and the observed supervision. The authors call these weights the standard form of the supervision, making the relationship between training information and evaluation explicit.

The required weights do not always exist, so the construction has a substantive applicability condition. The paper shows that previous ranking consistency results concerned special cases where they do exist. It also evaluates a new pairwise loss consistent with Discounted Cumulative Gain and its normalized form on benchmark datasets, connecting the general analysis to a concrete ranking objective.
icml-2011-learning-scoring-functions-wit.tldr: Order-preserving ranking losses can align training with evaluation metrics when suitable supervision-dependent weights exist.

paragraphs: The paper addresses prediction problems in which an example can receive several labels and those labels belong to a hierarchy. The hierarchy may be a tree or a directed acyclic graph. The authors aim to exploit these dependencies while producing a label combination that is consistent with the hierarchy’s structure.

Their key step is to express the search for the best consistent label combination as a search for the best subgraph. A simple greedy strategy solves the resulting problem, and theoretical results guarantee optimality for the proposed formulation. The method supports both hierarchy types, extending beyond approaches that use only tree-structured dependencies.

The authors describe the algorithm as efficient, easy to implement, suitable for large hierarchies, and free of the identified insufficient or skewed training-data problem in classifier training. Across numerous functional-genomics datasets, it consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art method on both trees and directed acyclic graphs. These results support the practical value of the subgraph formulation in the evaluated classification setting.
icml-2011-multilabel-classification-on-t.tldr: Hierarchical multi-label prediction becomes a best-subgraph problem, enabling efficient greedy inference with an optimality guarantee for trees and DAGs.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning reduces labeling demands by assigning labels to bags of examples rather than to every individual example. This paper questions the usual treatment of a bag as a finite collection. For applications involving images or audio, the authors argue that a low-dimensional manifold in a high-dimensional feature space can be a better representation.

Under this view, the geometry of a bag becomes relevant to learning. The paper shows that manifold structure affects PAC-learnability, connecting the shape of the represented data with formal learning guarantees. The change in representation therefore has consequences beyond how examples are stored: it affects the theoretical account of what can be learned.

The authors explain how an algorithm designed for finite bags can be adapted to manifold bags. They also propose a simple heuristic to reduce such algorithms’ memory requirements. Experiments on real-world data support the analysis and show that the approach works well, bringing together a geometric modeling argument, learnability analysis, and a practical adaptation of existing learning methods.
icml-2011-multiple-instance-learning-wit.tldr: Modeling multiple-instance bags as manifolds reveals geometric effects on learnability and motivates practical adaptations with reduced memory requirements.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to separate a noisy observed matrix into two structured components. One component is approximately low rank; the other has a complementary low-dimensional structure. The goal is to estimate both components despite observational noise, using estimators obtained by solving a convex optimization problem.

The authors establish a general theorem bounding the estimation error measured in Frobenius norm, which summarizes discrepancies across matrix entries. They then specialize the theorem to two settings associated with robust principal component analysis: a low-rank matrix combined with an entrywise sparse matrix, and a low-rank matrix combined with a column-sparse matrix.

The results cover deterministic and stochastic noise. In the stochastic case, the error bounds are minimax optimal, meaning they achieve the best worst-case statistical rates for the considered settings. Numerical simulations also confirm the sharpness of the theoretical predictions. The contribution links a tractable convex estimation approach to precise recovery-error guarantees across multiple forms of structured matrix decomposition.
icml-2011-noisy-matrix-decomposition-via.tldr: Convex matrix-decomposition estimators receive general error bounds that attain minimax-optimal rates in the analyzed stochastic-noise settings.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent solves an optimization problem through updates to individual coordinates, an arrangement that can appear inherently sequential. This paper introduces Shotgun, a parallel version for losses with L1 regularization. It asks how much simultaneous updating can accelerate these problems while preserving a theoretical account of convergence.

The authors prove convergence bounds that predict linear speedups up to a limit determined by the particular problem. That limit is central to the result: the analysis supports useful parallelism without claiming that speed will continue increasing proportionally as more updates run at once. The theory provides a prediction of the available acceleration.

A comprehensive empirical study evaluates Shotgun on Lasso and sparse logistic regression. The predicted potential for parallelism closely matches observed behavior on real data, and Shotgun outperforms other published solvers on a range of large problems. These findings connect the convergence analysis to practical scalability and support Shotgun as an effective solver for the evaluated L1-regularized tasks.
icml-2011-parallel-coordinate-descent-fo.tldr: Shotgun parallelizes coordinate descent with convergence bounds predicting linear speedups up to a problem-dependent limit, supported by large-scale experiments.

paragraphs: Probabilistic Matrix Addition models real-valued matrices while capturing covariance among both rows and columns. It adds two latent matrices, one drawn from a Gaussian process over rows and the other from a Gaussian process over columns. This construction brings both types of relationships into the same probabilistic model.

The resulting distribution does not split into independent pieces at the entry, row, or column level, allowing it to express intricate matrix dependencies. Exact inference is possible, but it requires large matrix inversions that can make computation prohibitive. The paper therefore distinguishes the model’s representational capacity from the cost of directly performing inference.

To make inference more practical, the authors exploit sparse dependencies among the latent variables. They propose two families of approximate algorithms, based respectively on Gibbs sampling and maximum a posteriori inference. Applications to missing-value prediction and multi-label classification demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution combines a joint row-and-column dependency model with computational approaches designed to make that model usable.
icml-2011-probabilistic-matrix-addition-.tldr: Probabilistic Matrix Addition combines row and column Gaussian-process structure, with approximate inference for prediction and classification tasks.

paragraphs: Matrix completion attempts to infer missing entries from an incompletely observed matrix. This paper studies the added difficulty of columns containing arbitrary corruption. The motivation is severe: standard completion algorithms can produce arbitrarily poor results even when only one column has been corrupted, making column-level contamination a consequential source of failure.

The authors investigate the case of many corrupted columns, including a constant fraction of the matrix’s columns, and develop a robust, efficient algorithm for the problem. A central feature of their results is that they impose no assumptions on the observed entries of the manipulated columns. The corrupt observations are therefore not required to follow a specified benign pattern.

Robust collaborative filtering provides a direct application. In that setting, some users act as manipulators who try to skew the system’s predictions. The paper connects this adversarial behavior to corrupted columns in matrix completion. Its contribution addresses the recovery problem while explicitly allowing unrestricted observed entries within those manipulated columns.
icml-2011-robust-matrix-completion-and-c.tldr: The paper develops robust matrix completion for corrupted columns without assumptions on the observed entries within the manipulated columns.

paragraphs: The paper formulates link prediction as an output-kernel learning problem. It uses semi-supervised Output Kernel Regression to address prediction when only a small portion of the available data is labeled. This places the relationships represented on the output side of the regression model at the center of the proposed approach.

The mathematical foundation uses reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces with vector-valued functions. Within that framework, the authors establish a new representer theorem for semi-supervised least-squares regression. They then use the theorem to derive Penalized Output Kernel Regression, or POKR, connecting the theoretical result directly to a model for the link-prediction task.

Numerical experiments cover artificial networks and two real applications, using a very low proportion of labeled data. The evaluation is transductive, so the reported relevance concerns predictions within that setting. The paper’s contribution combines a new regression theorem with an application model and empirical evidence that output-kernel learning can be useful for link prediction under sparse supervision.
icml-2011-semi-supervised-penalized-outp.tldr: POKR derives a semi-supervised output-kernel model for link prediction and demonstrates relevance with very little labeled data in transductive experiments.

paragraphs: The paper introduces LSE-RMax, a model-based algorithm for learning structure in ergodic factored-state Markov decision processes. Factored states describe the environment through multiple components, making the dependencies governing transitions part of the learning problem. The algorithm addresses this setting without requiring the transition function’s in-degree to be supplied beforehand.

The in-degree concerns how many inputs participate in a transition dependency. Removing the need for prior knowledge of it reduces the structural information that must be given to the learner. The main guarantee is conditional: when the planning horizon satisfies a stated condition, LSE-RMax achieves a return very close to optimal with high certainty.

The authors fully implement the algorithm and provide a detailed sample-complexity analysis, examining the data demands of learning. They also report empirical effectiveness compared with prior approaches. The contribution combines structure learning, a conditional near-optimality guarantee, and an implemented method, with the guarantee explicitly situated in ergodic factored environments and the required planning-horizon condition.
icml-2011-structure-learning-in-ergodic-.tldr: LSE-RMax learns factored MDP structure without a supplied transition in-degree and guarantees near-optimal return under a planning-horizon condition.

paragraphs: The paper develops a convolutional factor-analysis model that infers how many filters, or factors, to use. It employs a beta process for single-task learning and a hierarchical beta process for multi-task learning. The number of filters is therefore treated as something to infer within the model, alongside its other parameters.

Parameter computation takes place in a Bayesian framework using Gibbs sampling. The authors explicitly exploit the convolutional structure of the expansion to accelerate computation. This connects the model’s mathematical organization to its implementation: the convolutional form contributes both to the representation and to how the required calculations are carried out.

The model is also used in a multi-level, deep analysis of general data. The abstract identifies image-processing datasets, including classification, as concrete applications for which results are presented. The contribution brings together inferred filter counts, single-task and multi-task formulations, and a multi-level analysis. Its stated computational contribution is the use of convolutional structure to speed Bayesian parameter computation.
icml-2011-the-hierarchical-beta-process-.tldr: A Bayesian convolutional factor model infers filter counts with beta processes and supports multi-task and deep analyses.

paragraphs: The paper asks why sparse coding has performed better than traditional vector quantization for visual recognition. Both approaches involve learning a dictionary from unlabeled data and then using that dictionary to encode new inputs as features. The authors separate these stages to determine which contributes most to the observed performance.

Experiments on CIFAR, NORB, and Caltech 101 compare multiple dictionary-training and encoding combinations. These include vector quantization paired with a soft-threshold activation function. Decoupling training from encoding allows the study to examine whether an effective feature representation depends primarily on how the dictionary was obtained or on how it is subsequently used.

The results show that fast vector-quantization training can be used without a performance penalty in the studied comparisons, and that randomly selected training examples can also serve as dictionaries. Choosing a good encoder matters more in these experiments; it can often be a simple feed-forward nonlinearity. The paper also reports state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR and NORB, supporting the effectiveness of this emphasis on encoding.
icml-2011-the-importance-of-encoding-ver.tldr: Controlled visual-recognition experiments find that encoder choice matters more than sophisticated dictionary training, with strong results from simple alternatives.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical topic model using nonparametric Bayesian methods. Its hierarchy allows a child topic to have multiple parents, with the aim of avoiding redundant subtopics deeper in the structure. This gives the model a way to represent a subtopic shared across broader topics without requiring a separate copy under each.

A second design feature reduces repeated use of words across multiple scales, producing more parsimonious subtopics. The prior places no fixed bound on the hierarchy’s depth or width. A retrospective sampler adaptively infers an appropriate size from the corpus, making the extent of the hierarchy responsive to the documents being modeled.

The authors report excellent quantitative results on five standard datasets and find the inferred structures highly interpretable. These findings support both the model’s measured performance and the usefulness of its topic organization in the evaluated collections. The contribution combines flexible hierarchy size with explicit mechanisms aimed at reducing redundancy in subtopics and their word usage.
icml-2011-topic-modeling-with-nonparamet.tldr: A nonparametric hierarchical topic model infers its size while allowing shared subtopics and reducing redundant word use across levels.
